sentences.text: Coccosteus was a small placoderm, with the species C. cuspidatus measuring between 29.6 and 39.4 cm in length.
This fish possessed a joint between the armor of its body and skull, a trait shared with other arthrodires.
The animal kept its beak sharp by having the edges of its dental plates grind against each other.
Although Coccosteus looked similar to the giant Dunkleosteus, its eyes were positioned closer to the end of its snout.
While the largest specimens reached about 40 cm, the average length was between 20 and 24 cm.
The species C. cuspidatus serves as an important index fossil in the Devonian sequence of northern Scotland's Orcadian Basin.
The genus Coccosteus was described by Agassiz in 1843.
Likely the best-known arthrodire, up to 49 species have been identified since its initial description, many later reclassified.
Coccosteus could feed on fairly large prey due to its longer jaws and wide-opening mouth.
The up-and-down movement of Coccosteus's skull allowed more water to be pumped through its gills.
Researchers suggest Coccosteus may have supplemented its diet by filtering organic material from mud using its gills.
Coccosteus is the type genus for the family Coccosteidae, which belongs to the clade Coccosteomorphi within Eubrachythoraci.
Coccosteus lived during the Middle to Late Devonian periods.
Fossils of Coccosteus have been found throughout Europe and North America.
Most fossils are found in freshwater sediments, suggesting the animal may have occasionally entered saltwater.
